title: Sixty-Four Kilobytes, and Every Abstraction That Hid It
content:
Both the Z80 and the 6502 had a sixteen-bit address bus, which means 64 KB, and essentially every interesting design decision in the 8-bit world is a consequence of that number. The first machine you build is a 32 KB one. The second one is 64 KB. The third machine is 128 KB, and it exists because the address bus is full, and the design problem has changed shape entirely.
The term for the workaround is bank switching, and it is worth understanding properly because it is a real memory model with real rules, not a trick.
The Spectrum’s version. The Z80 can address 64 KB directly. The 128K Spectrum had 128 KB, so the extra 80 KB became five pages of 16 KB mapped into the top of the address space, selected by writing to a port. The same mechanism paged the 16 KB BASIC ROM in and out at the bottom, which is why a Spectrum program can be sitting in RAM and still be running code that thinks it is in ROM.
The consequence for a programmer is not just "there is more memory". It is that the memory is a resource you swap, and anything you point at may become invalid when you change the page. Code that holds a pointer across a bank switch is the 8-bit equivalent of a use-after-free, and it was a genuinely common bug.
The C64’s version, which is stranger. The C64 uses the 6510, which is a 6502 with extra I/O pins on the package, and those pins are wired directly to the memory map. You can reconfigure the address space by writing a byte to location $01.
Write the right value there and almost the whole 64 KB becomes RAM, with the system ROMs and the I/O area switched out. The same register swaps BASIC and the KERNAL together, because the machine is designed so the two are consistent. Memory under a ROM could always be written but not read back, which sounds like a bug and is actually the reason the machine feels fast: the KERNAL and the video chip both read RAM, and the design keeps them from contending for the bus.
The CPC’s version, and the cost of the design. The Amstrad CPC ran a 4 MHz Z80A and delivered about 3.3 MHz of it, because the video hardware demanded the CPU wait on microsecond boundaries. Memory access is padded so the display does not snow. That is a bus contention tax of roughly a fifth of your processor, paid continuously, and it was the standard trade in home computers of that era.
Acorn’s answer, which is the interesting one. The BBC Micro specified a flat memory model where the CPU and the video could both touch RAM without contention, and Steve Furber pushed hard for DRAM fast enough to make it work at the time, which was genuinely hard and not available from anyone else. The BBC had asked for a Z80 running CP/M. Acorn delivered a 6502 with a proprietary OS instead, and added the Tube as a concession: an expansion interface for a second processor, so a Z80 could run CP/M alongside.
That is the shape of the decision. Acorn lost the specification and won the architecture.
Why I care about this professionally. These machines have no memory protection, no scheduler, and no abstraction between you and the bus. Every abstraction we have added since has a name and a cost that somebody paid, and reading about these designs is a good corrective to the assumption that any of it came for free. The bank-switching bug is a use-after-free. The CPC’s contention is a bad bus arbitration decision. The BBC’s flat memory model is a NUMA problem solved early by refusing to have one.
None of it is nostalgia. It is the same set of trade-offs, in a machine small enough to hold in your head, which is exactly the property we keep claiming to want and rarely get back.
